sentences: This is The Kiss by Gustav Klimt.
On a square canvas 180 centimetres on each side, two lovers wrapped in golden robes embrace at the edge of a flowering meadow.
The whole surface glows with a soft golden light.
Klimt was the son of a gold engraver and grew up around the craft of working gold.
Painted in 1907 and 1908, this picture is the high point of what is called his Golden Period, when gold became central to his art.
Look at the two heads.
The man, crowned with vines, turns his face away from us as he kisses her cheek.
She wears a crown of flowers, her face tilted upward and her eyes quietly closed.
Only their faces are left as living skin.
His hands cradle her face, while hers hold on to his neck and his hand.
Notice how realistic faces and hands live side by side with flat ornament on the very same surface.
That contrast is the heart of Klimt's style.
The man's robe is filled with black and white rectangles.
These straight, angular shapes set up a firm, strong rhythm inside the gold.
Stacked one above another, they can look almost like a column of stone.
The woman's dress is full of round flowers and circles in red, blue and violet.
The two patterns overlap within one golden form, expressing the moment two people become one.
Straight lines and curves embrace each other, just like the lovers.
Lower right, look at her bare feet as she kneels.
Her toes curl over the very edge where the meadow drops away into nothing.
So in this kiss, ecstasy and danger are felt together, as if the moment could tip over at any second.
Flecks of gold are scattered across the dark background like dust floating in a beam of light.
On a trip to Italy in 1903, Klimt saw the Byzantine mosaics of San Vitale in Ravenna and deeply admired their flatness and golden brilliance.
So he laid real gold leaf over the oil paint and added silver and platinum too.
The surface glows like a mosaic in a church.
Move a little to one side, and the shimmer changes with the light and your position.
It was first shown in 1908 at the Kunstschau exhibition in Vienna, and the Austrian state bought it even before it was finished.
Beloved from the very start, it now hangs in the Belvedere in Vienna.
Step back, and the couple becomes a single golden shape.
Can you trace where his squares and her circles meet and melt into each other?
You may find the border is harder to see than you expect.
